A Hasib with Kamal Ziaul Islam Advocates ----- For the Petitioner (In Writ Petition Nos. 4607 & 4608). 
Raisudin Ahmed, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No. 7. 
AJ Mohammad Ali, Additional Attorney-General, Adilur Rahman Khan, Deputy Attorney-General with Razik Al-Jalil, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For Government Respondents. 
AKM Shamsul Karim, Advocate ----- For Respondent No.3 (In all the Writ Petitions).
parties:
Ekushey Television Ltd and another ------ Petitioners
Vs
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
12. Respondent No.3, BTRC, has filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that it was not the licensing authority for broadcasting. And it could only allocate the frequency once such a licence was obtained from the Ministry of Information in view of the provision of sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Bangladesh Telecommunications Act, 2001, shortly, the Act of 2001. The petitioners' application dated 6-5-2003 filed to the BTRC was thus misconceived' And was like putting the cart before the horse. The position of law being such, the Writ Petition is ex-facie misconceived, devoid of any cause of action And not maintainable in the eye of law. The impugned letter (Annexure- C-1) bearing memo No. BTRC/PROSHA: DO/2002-1333(2); dated 7-6-2003 was issued improperly without following the procedure of decision making. Subsequently, in view of its impropriety, the said letter has been withdrawn by BTRC vide memo No. BTRC/Prosha: DO/ 2002/1391, dated 26-6-2003 on the advice of the learned Attorney-General for Bangladesh. Since the impugned letter has already been withdrawn the Rule has become infructuous. A supplementary affidavit-in-opposition has also been filed on behalf of respondent No. 3 stating, inter alia, that section 3(2) of the Act of 2001 had put an embargo upon issuance of any broadcasting licence by the BTRC And section 36 And section 38 of the said Act only refers to the issuance of licence to establish or operate telecommunication in Bangladesh, ie to issue licence to mobile phone companies as contemplated under section 35(a)(b) And (c) of Bangladesh Telecommunication Act, 2001. The provision to section 3(1)(ii) authorises the respondent only to allocate the frequency for television station or broadcasting apparatus, or control of the allocated frequency. 

 15. The petitioner has also filed an affidavit- in-reply against the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent No. 2 stating, inter alia, that television was a state monopoly until 2001. The electronic media, radio And television, had until 2001 operated under a colonial legal framework provided by the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933. In order to bring about a basic change in the legal framework to conform to the requirements of a democratic constitution, which guarantees freedom of the electronic media, the drafting of a new law to deal with private television broadcasting, was undertaken pursuant to the National Telecommunication Policy, 1998. The Act of 2001 provided for a new regulatory framework for telecommunications, including radio And television, by establishing an independent Regulatory Commission. Television broadcasting was, intended by the Act of 2001 to be regulated by BTRC which would exercise those powers as per the provisions of sections 36 And 55 of the 2001 Act. ETV Ltd operating as a private television station, when the 2001 Act came into force on 31st January, 2001, And upon its coming into force, it attracted the provisions of sections 89 And 91 of that Act. Section 89 of the Act provides, inter alia, that certain matters under the Telegraph Act of 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 were to be vested in the Commission. Section 91 of the 2001 Act provides that radio frequency allocated before commencement of the Act was to continue for limited period until the Commission had allocated the frequency on the basis of an application filed before it. Before coming into force of the Act of 2001, the petitioner had been using the frequencies allocated by the Frequency And Wireless Board And paying licence fee And royalty fee pursuant to the 1885 And 1933 Acts. The petitioner had paid licence fee And royalty fee for the TV transmitter And wireless equipment in 2000 And 2001 pursuant to demAnd notes issued by the Ministry of Post And Telecommunication dated 3-4-2000, 25-2-2001 And 13-3-2001. When the licence fee for the Wireless equipment And transmitter became due the petitioner ETV Limited by its letter dated 30-1-2002 applied for issuance of a demAnd note for licence fee And royalty fee; in response to that letter the petitioner was informed that it was BTRC which was vested with authority to grant/renew licence for the wireless equipment. BTRC published a Public Notice in newspapers, in particular in the Daily Ittefaque dated 3-3-2002, inviting applications from those who were using frequencies to make payment for the frequencies in accordance with the provisions of the Act of 2001. The petitioner by its letters, in particular letter dated 7-4-2002 applied to BTRC for payment for licence fee And frequency charges for using wireless broadcasting equipment. In response to the letter dated 7-4-2002 BTRC communicated bye-mail dated 8-6-2002 requesting the petitioner company to send the details of payment of licence fees, etc. BTRC sent another e-mail dated 6-7-2002 requesting the petitioner to submit the documents regarding payment of licence fee And other related documentation. The petitioner in support of its application submitted all the relevant documents to BTRC regarding payment of licence fee And royalty for the use of broadcasting equipment by its letter dated 12-6-2002. The petitioner also furnished details of the broadcasting equipment by its letter dated 7-7-2002. Thereafter, the petitioner sent another letter on 15-7-2002 along with account payee cheques as licence fee for the broadcasting equipment. Thus, it was amply evident from the above facts that the petitioner's application for licence under the Act of 2001 was being processed, And upon this being pointed out, the Appellate Division made clear observations in its judgment disposing of Civil Review Petition Nos. 78, 79 And 80 of 2002 to the effect that the judgment would have no bearing in considering the application by Ekushey by BTRC which is free to decide in accordance with law. It was in the above context that the petitioner was taken by surprise when it received BTRC's letter dated 7-6-2003, where it was stated that BTRC could not grant the licence on the misconceived plea that the Appellate Division judgment stood in the way of such action. The petitioner thereupon moved the instant writ petition challenging the said letter And obtained the Rule. BTRC played a dubious role by sending a letter dated 26-6-2003 to the petitioner stating that it withdrew the letter dated 7-6-2003. But soon after that BTRC filed an application for disposal of the writ petition on the alleged ground that the letter dated 7-6-2003 having been withdrawn the Writ Petition has become infructuous. BTRC thereafter, filed an Affidavit-in-opposition on 5-8-2003 taking a new position that it is not the licensing authority for broadcasting but it can only allocate the frequency, once licence is obtained. The new position taken by BTRC was untenable And misconceived inasmuch as the provisions under which power was exercised for issuing licence to private television viz. section 4 of the Telegraph Act, 1885 And section 5 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, were expressly now conferred upon the BTRC which has been given exclusive authority in this regard by the Act of 2001. Since there is only one company, ie ETV Ltd, which is the petitioner the licence will be granted to the company. As regards who will represent or be authorised to receive the licence And the apparatus, this can fully be dealt with by the Board of Directors, who, without any difficulty, can And would authorise the natural person or persons to whom the licence And the apparatus should be delivered. The minority shareholders, And in particular Mr Nasir A Chowdhury, who has belatedly come forward after doing nothing for even six months to keep ETV Limited afloat or injected any money for its operations nor even to attend or call any Board meeting, cannot, in law, create or be permitted to create obstruction to the grant of a licence to ETV Ltd. 

 16. Two supplementary affidavits have also been filed by the petitioner stating, inter alia that a meeting of the Board of Directors of the petitioner company was convened on 30-12-2002 in the presence of quorum. The meeting was presided over by the then Chairman Mr AS Mahmud who submitted his resignation as Chairman of the Board. Mr Abdus Salam by virtue of being the single largest shareholder of the Company And with the support of 75% of the Company's total shareholding was elected as the new Chairman And Chief Executive Officer of the petitioner company. In the said meeting the Board unanimously approved the transfer of shares by a foreign investor, Citicorp International Finance Corporation ("CIFC"), in the name of Mr Abdus Salam. The "Particulars of Directors, Managing Agents" (Form XII) was subsequently presented for filing by Mr Abdus Salam, chairman of the petitioner company on 30-12-2002 in accordance with section 115 of the Companies Act, 1994. In the said meeting Mr Abdus Salam was also authorised to negotiate with the Government And other bodies to obtain approval from the competent authority to commence broadcasting which was stopped on 29-8-2002. Since taking over the post of chairman And chief executive officer of the company Mr Abdus Salam has presided over the board meetings And extraordinary general meetings. The meetings were conducted according to the Articles of Association of the petitioner company And by serving of the required notices to all the directors/shareholders of the Company. The elected Chairman And Chief Executive Officer of the Company Mr Abdus Salam has taken exemplary measures to sustain the petitioner company's existence. Immediately following the disposal of the review petitions, all the Company's bank accounts were frozen by the syndication lenders led by StAndard Chartered Bank. Since being elected chairman And chief executive officer Mr Abdus Salam has been single- hAndedly bearing all the operational expenses of the Company including salaries of 180 employees, maintenance of the costly And highly sophisticated broadcasting And transmission equipment, office rent And other expenses, utilities, totalling an amount of Taka 70 lac per month which is being spent from Mr Abdus Salam's own sources where no revenue or income is being generated by the petitioner company. Immediately following his election as the chairman of the petitioner company, Mr Salam started correspondence with various ministries of the Government And other bodies in order to re-establish the terrestrial And satellite transmission in favour of the petitioner company. In that regard Mr Salam had submitted application dated 20-2-2003 to the Information Minister with copies to the Secretary, Ministry of information And the Chairman of BTRC for according permission for terrestrial And satellite transmission in favour of the petitioner company. Similarly, he also submitted a prayer to the Prime Minister dated 23-2-2003 for her kind And sympathetic consideration over the same issue. During this period none of the local directors took any steps towards the revival of the petitioner company's broadcasting operation. Mr Abdus Salam made an application on 6-5-2003 to the BTRC for accordance of broadcasting permission in favour of the petitioner company in the interest of public welfare. The petitioner received a reply from the BTRC dated 7-6-2003 stating that since the licence granted by the Government had already been cancelled by the High Court in Writ Petition No. 5050 of 2001 And the same was upheld by the Appellate Division there was no scope for consideration of the petitioners' application for granting permission to commence satellite broadcasting. The issuance of the Rule Nisi in the Writ Petition prompted interested quarters to come forward in creating obstruction in the legal proceedings. One of the directors, holding 4.17% shares of the petitioner company, Mr Nasir A Chowdhury filed an application for addition of party as a respondent purportedly claiming himself to be the Chairman of the company. Such an application was manifestly a malafide step at the instance of interested quarters to obstruct the speedy disposal of the matter which was followed by the filing of another writ petition being Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2003 making the same prayers. Mr Abdus Salam has been running the company since the beginning of this year And under his outstAnding leadership the Company is now looking forward to commence its broadcasting operation. He has not only been attending the office of the petitioner company regularly, but also been taking interest in all the Company's affairs And presiding over all decision- making meetings regarding its programmes, marketing, distribution, finance, etc. Mr Salam diligently meets with all the Company's staff, enquiring after their welfare And motivating them in these difficult times. Although Mr Salam is a non resident Bangladeshi residing in Germany for the past 21 years where he runs several highly successful business operations, he has left his home And business in Germany, And is spending all his time And efforts with the sole objective of reviving the petitioner company. In stark contrast to Mr Salam's efforts, some of the Company's directors, including Mr Nasir A Choudhury, have done nothing to help the petitioner company. During the last eight months Mr Nasir A Choudhury has not even visited the company's office premises for one day. The claim of Mr Nasir A Choudhury that he was elected Chairman of the petitioner company on 8-9-2002 is illegal. The facts are that on 8-9-2002 due to a lack of quorum And in the absence of the then Chairman Mr AS Mahmud no meeting could be held as would be evident from the copy of minutes of the meeting of the board of directors held on 8-9-2002 annexed to the Affidavit. The petitioner made references to Article 41 of the Articles of Association of the petitioner company which required that a resolution to elect a Chairman may only be ratified with the consent of75% of the Directors. In the so-called resolution by circulation dated 8-9-2002 on the basis of which Mr Nasir A Choudhury claims Chairmanship of the Company, there were not enough required signatures or approvals by the Directors. The meeting of the Board of Directors held on 30-12-2002 in London approved the transfer of shares by CIFC in the name of Mr Abdus Salam which had been discussed in the board meeting held on 30-12-2002. Before the said meeting a seven days notice of the board meeting was issued to all Directors on 21-12-2002 in accordance with Article 40 of the Articles of Association of the petitioner company. The board meeting dated 30-12-2002 was held in London due to the fact that over 50% of the board of directors were present in London at that time. This included the presence of the 2 sponsor directors, one each foreign And local investors which were necessary to form quorum of the board meeting. Mr Nasir A Choudhury telephoned Mr Salam And the employees of the petitioner company And threatened that he will forcibly occupy the office premises And oust the employees And management executives. This created genuine apprehension in the mind of Mr Salam, And he, finding no other alternative And being seriously intimidated, formally informed the local police station by filing a GD entry on 17-7- 2003. Mr Nasir A Choudhury, so-called chairman, at the behest of an interested quarter And only to disturb And damage the existence of the petitioner company And its Chairman Mr Abdus Salam has filed Writ Petitions No. 4608 of 2003 And 4607 of 2003 And Title Suit No. 143 of 2003 on 28-5-2003 in the Court of 4th Joint District Judge, Dhaka, which is being contested by the legal Chairman Mr Abdus Salam. While BTRC was claiming that it did not have the authority to issue a licence as per section 3 of the Act of 2001, it had on the application of international Television (Pvt) Ltd/NTV, issued a licence/permission on 19-2-2003. It is obvious from the aforesaid letter granting permission/licence on 19-2-2003 that respondent No. 3 is the existing authority, for issuance of a broadcast licence. Subsequently, on 1-2-2003 apost facto release order was issued by respondent No.2 (Ministry of Information) to NTV And on 30-1-2003 another letter was issued by the same, which has been referred to as No Objection Certificate. After the closure of ETV on 29-8-2002, the chairman of the petitioner company filed several applications to respondents No. 3 And 2 including the Hon'ble Prime Minister with a request that necessary action be taken in respect of the petitioner's application for a licence. When no action was taken on the aforesaid applications the chairman of the Petitioner Company filed another application on 8-5-2003 before respondent No. 3 along with a prescribed form. But respondent No.3 without assigning any reason kept the application dated 8-5-2003 unattended while rejecting the application of ETV dated 6-5-2003 vide its letter dated 7-6-2003. The instant writ petition having been filed by the petitioner company impugning the aforesaid rejection order of respondent No.3, copy of the application dated 8-5-2003 in prescribed form was not annexed to the petition. Since a question has arisen during the hearing of the instant writ petition whether ETV had filed necessary application for a licence in prescribed form, it has become necessary to file the affidavit stating that ETV had already submitted application for licence dated 8-5-2003 in the prescribed form to BTRC (respondent No.3) And to annex a copy thereof. 

 22. He submitted that BTRC, established under the Act of 2001, has been given a free hAnd to decide the application filed by any person, here the petitioner, ETV Ltd, for allocating the frequency to air the programmes, And its plea, that under section 3(2) of the Act, 2001 it had/has no jurisdiction to give licence allocating frequencies for the purpose of broadcasting unless a licence is obtained from the Ministry of Information, is based on total misconception of law. He submitted that proviso to section 3(2) of the Act of 2001 clearly authorises the BTRC to issue licence in respect of all the matters mentioned in the said section including allocating frequency to broadcast the programme through a satellite channel. He further submitted that ETV Ltd was a going concern And although this court in the earlier writ petition declared the licence of ETV Ltd to have been issued illegally And without lawful authority, the persons who were responsible for obtaining such illegal licence are no more in the Company And now the Company is being run by new faces, particularly Mr Abdus Salam as its Chairman And Managing Director who has invested a huge amount of money to ensure that ETV Ltd runs properly, the BTRC was legally bound to consider the application in a positive way And by not doing so it has failed to perform its statutory obligation And therefore, acted without jurisdiction. He submitted that Act of 2001 came into force on 31-1-2001 providing for a new regulatory framework for telecommunication And for the establishment of an independent Commission for the purpose of development And effect regulation of telecommunication system And telecommunication services in Bangladesh And matters ancillary thereto. It cannot be conceived that after coming into force of the said Act, the petitioner or any other person who wishes to establish a satellite channel to broadcast its programme would have to proceed under the provisions of the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 for a licence for the purpose as contended by respondent No.3. By referring to various definitions as given in section 2 of the Act of 2001, particularly the definition of telecommunication system And proviso to section 3(2) of the Act, he submitted that the Commission being independent it has the right And privilege to grant licence to operate a satelite channel including allocation of frequency for such radio station or television station or broadcasting apparatus, or control of the allocated frequency or broadcasting apparatus or use of telecommunication apparatus for the purpose of broadcasting, And cannot shun its responsibilities in not considering the applications of the petitioner filed at different times, besides the one dated 6-5-2003. In elaborating his submission he has also referred to sections 35, 36, 38 And 55 of the Act of 2001 And further submitted that with the emergence of the new law it was not necessary to approach the Ministry for a licence for running a television station through a sate1\ite channel to broadcast the programme. Dr Hossain by referring to the various annexures filed with the affidavit in reply dated 11-8-2003 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent No.2 vide Annexures S,T,U, U(1),V, V(1) And W series submitted that after the Act of 2001 came into force the petitioner applied to the authority to regularise the transmission facilities given to it earlier as per the provision of section 89 of the Act, but the authority did not consider the representation illegally. He also referred to various letters vide Annexures R series received from BTRC by which the petitioner had been instructed by it to furnish relevant documents And other details of the Company And the payments that were subsequently made by the petitioner by way of licensing fees And other charges, but even then it did not give the necessary licence to use the frequencies through a satelite channel And, therefore, it is necessary to give a direction upon the BTRC in that respect. Dr Hossain submitted that it is the company, ETV who is the petitioner in all the writ petitions And the licence for the frequencies required to broadcast its programmes through a satelite channel shall be given to the company And on behalf of the company the authorised person shall receive the same. He in this regard further submitted that the conflict between the two directors of the company can very much be settled in a board meeting And that cannot be a ground to refuse the giving of the required licence to it. He also submitted that Mr Nasir A Chowdhury is the owner of only 4.17% shares of the company And that from annexure N to the supplementary affidavit it is clear that in the meeting, of the Board of Directors of the company held on 30-10-2002 presided over by Mr Nasir A Chowdhury transfer of shares by CIFC to Mr Abdus Salam was approved. Annexure G, the proceeding of the board meeting shows that a meeting of the company was held on 30-12-2002 in which Mr Salam was appointed as the new chairman And chief executive officer of the company. Further, the impugned order that was passed on the application filed by him prima facie show that he is the chairman of the company And he can very much represent the company And can very much receive the licence on its behalf. Doctor Hossain also submitted that the act of seizure of the machineries/equipment of the petitioner as detailed in the Rule issuing order by respondent No. 1 through respondent Nos. 8 And 9 (Annexures F And F1) was unwarranted And malafide as no circumstances as provided in section 5 of the Telegraph Act, 1885 existed at the time of seizure of the said equipment. He also lastly, submitted that the respondents acted malafide in not returning the equipment which are very sophisticated in nature even after the filing of the application as per observation made by this court in Writ Petition No. 4564 of 2002 And, as such, the action of the respondents is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority And is of no legal effect And they are to be directed to return the machineries And equipment’s to the petitioner company forthwith. 

 there was no scope to consider the prayer to give the frequency to the petitioner to run the satellite television as has been contended in the application (Annexure C). Learned Additional Attorney-General lastly, submitted that the petitioner, however, if at all interested to run the satellite television having the required frequency from the BTRC, would first have to apply to the Ministry of Information under the provisions of the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act 1933 to have a licence for the purpose And unless it does so it cannot have any relief from this Court. In support of his submission he referred to various sections of the Act of 2001 And mainly relied upon the provision of section 3(2) to show that no power lies with the BTRC to grant licence for any broadcasting, radio broadcasting station or a television broadcasting station or licensing of such station broadcasting apparatus or an apparatus for receiving any message or other information or a programme transmitted by way of broadcast, or the business of such apparatus. In conclusion he submitted that the petitioner having not approached the concerned Ministry for such a licence after the judgment And order passed in the review petitions by the Appellate Division upholding the declaration made by the High Court Division that granting of licence to ETV was done without lawful authority And is of no legal effect the petitioner has no cause of action to maintain the writ petitions And no mAndate as sought for can be given by this court. 

 without making any positive prayer in the form of consequential relief for a direction upon the defendants to give the frequencies And the licence required to broadcast the programme of ETV And to return the seized equipment to it. It is also to be noted that Writ Petition No. 3488 of 2003 challenging the seizure of the machineries of ETV filed by Mr Abdus Salam was first moved before this court on 19-5-2003 but on the prayer of the learned Attorney-General the hearing was adjourned till one week after the ensuing vacation. And eventually, Rule was issued on 1-7-2003 as already noted at the beginning of the judgment. Mr Nasir A Chowdhury as it appears from the order sheets of the respective writ petition moved this court in its writ jurisdiction on 12-7-2003 And 14-7-2003 And obtained the Rules on those dates. Whereas, Mr Abdus Salam being the petitioner in Writ Petitions Nos. 4196 of 2003 And 3488 of 2003, with the petition affidavit-in-reply And the supplementary affidavits have annexed so many papers showing his vigilance And active steps taken in putting the ETV into action which will be considered at the relevant place of this judgment. Mr Salam has also annexed the resolution of the Board of Directors dated 30-12-2002 And the particulars of the Directors of the Company as on 30-12-2002 filed before the Registrar of the Joint Stock Companies under Form XII And the resignation of Mr Abu Sayed Mahmud as the Chairman of the Company on that date (Annexures-J And I respectively). In the supplementary affidavit dated 10-8-2003 filed in Writ Petition No. 4196 of 2003 the petitioner has categorically stated that the claim of Mr Nasir A Chowdhury that he was elected Chairman of the company on 8-9-2002 is illegal as on that date no meeting could be held due to lack of quorum And in the absence of the then chairman Mr AS Mahmud And in support of the said statements the resolution of the board meeting has been annexed as Annexure M. In the writ petition filed by Mr Nasir A Chowdhury as well as with the affidavit-in- opposition no paper has been filed showing his activities as the chairman of the company after he became its chairman as claimed by him. From the supplementary affidavit dated 10-8-2003 filed by the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4196 of 2003 it appears that Mr Abdus Salam filed an application on 16-7-2003 (Annexure-O) to BTRC for providing him necessary information as to whether any application was filed to it by Mr Nasir A Chowdhury on 29-5-2003 on behalf of ETV Ltd And if any application was filed then what decision was taken by it. Another application was filed on 27-7- 2003 by the secretary of the company (Annexure O-1) to let him know by 2-8-2003 as to whether any such application was filed by Mr Nasir A Choudhury failing which it would be deemed that no such application was filed, but no reply was given, which proves that, in fact, no application was filed by Mr Nasir A Chowdhury And this is further fortified from the statements made by respondent No.3 in its affidavit-in-opposition as quoted hereinbefore. From the statements made in the writ petitions, the affidavits-in-opposition And the supplementary affidavits it appears to us that in fact Mr Nasir A Chowdhury has come to this court only to join an issue, as to the chairmanship of the company And not for getting the licence for the frequency And the licence required to broadcast the programme of ETV And to get back the machineries seized. It prima facie appears to us that Mr' Abdus Salam has, in fact, been trying very hard for getting back the machineries of the ETV And also to get the frequencies And the licence required to broadcast its programme. From the papers filed by the parties as discussed it also, prima facie appears to us that, in fact, it is Mr Abdus Salam who has been functioning as the chairman of the company And chief executive officer And, as such, he has the locus stAndi to file the petitions in question on behalf of the company on And from 30-12-2002. Be that as it may, the whole question is as to who will get the licence to broadcast the programme; the company or the Chairman; obviously it is the company ETV Ltd And, as such, we do not see any difficulty on the part of the BTRC or the concerned Ministry (as argued by the learned Additional Attorney-General) And the other government officials to take decision in the matter. The company is a juristic person, there must be someone to act on its behalf, be it the Chairman of the company or its Managing Director as its Chief Executive. And any other authorised person of the company would be able to receive the licence And the machineries on its behalf And that is an internal matter of the, company. We hold that so far as the dispute as regards the Chairmanship of the company is concerned if cannot be a bar either on the part of the BTRC to decide the question of giving the frequency And the licence required to broadcast its programme And on the part of the other concerned respondents giving back the seized machineries/equipment to the company. Thus, we do not see the application of section 88 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the facts And the circumstances of these cases as argued by the learned Additional Attorney-General And the principle of law enunciated in the case referred by him. 

 28. Let -us now consider the submission of Doctor Hossain that ETV was a going concern And the people who were responsible for obtaining the licence in an unlawful manner, as, found earlier by this court in Writ Petition No. 5050 of 2001 And upheld by the Appellate Division, are no more in the company And it is now being run by a new set of persons And, as such, in view of the provision of sections 89, 90 And 91 of the Act of 2001, whatever might be the irregularities And the illegalities resorted to by the earlier management in obtaining the licence can be rectified And regularised by issuing fresh licence for the purpose. Doctor Hossain in support of his submission drew our attention to the newspaper advertisement dated 19-2-2002 made by BTRC vide Annexure T to the supplementary affidavit dated 11-8-2002, from which it appears that application was invited from the Radio frequency users to apply by 31-3-2002 for paying levy under the new rate. He also referred to the other annexures vide Annexure U series to show that as per the said advertisement ETV took step in the matter by making correspondence with BTRC And other relevant authority And, as such, mAndamus may be given to the BTRC to allocate the frequency And the licence required to broadcast the programme. This submission of Dr Hossain cannot be entertained. Mere reading of sections 89, 90 And 91 of the Act of 2001 show that those provisions have been made to protect the interest And the right of the persons who had an existing vested legal right on the basis of a validly obtained licence, certificate or permit or licensing agreement under the Telegraph Act, 1885 (XII of 1985) And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 (XVII of 1933), that is, before the Act of 2001 came into operation. In the instant case ETV started broadcasting its programme through terrestrial as well as satellite channel on the basis of a licensing agreement between the Ministry of Information And Mr AS Mahmud under the said old laws which has been declared to have been obtained without lawful authority And is of no legal effect in Writ Petition No. 5050 of 2001. Therefore, the petitioner cannot get any benefit of sections 89, 90 And 91 of the Act of 2001. In other words, the petitioner cannot bank upon any of its rights which accrued to it on the basis of an invalid licence obtained by it. But we are of the view that petitioner had/has legal And fundamental right to approach the authority concerned afresh under the provisions of the Act of 2001 which came into operation with effect from 31-1-2001 for allocating the frequencies And the licence required to broadcast its programme through a satellite channel. Moreso, the Appellate Division while disposing of the Civil Review petitions clearly observed that their judgment would have no bearing in considering the application filed by Ekushey Television for licence by the commission which would be free to decide in accordance with law. 

 29. Now the most pertinent And the crucial question to be decided in the context of the pleadings of the parties And the relevant law namely, the Act of 2001, the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 is, who is the authority to be approached for the allocation of the frequencies And the licence required to broadcast the programme through a satellite channel And as to whether the petitioner approached it. 

 30. The learned Additional Attorney-General strenuously argued that sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Act of 2001 does not authorise the BTRC to issue licence to any person for any broadcasting, a radio broadcasting station or a television broadcasting station or licensing of such station; broadcasting apparatus or for an apparatus for receiving any message or other information of a programme transmitted by way of broadcasting or the business of such apparatus but it is the Ministry of Information which is the authority to give the licence for the same under the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933. And the petitioner having wrongly approached the BTRC it is not entitled to get any mAndate as prayed for. In support or' his submission he has referred to the definition of 'broadcasting', 'interested party Licence spectrum Management Committee', 'Telecommunications', 'telecommunication system' as defined in section 2 of the Act of 2001 And also the definition of 'telegraph' And telegraph authority' in section 3 of the Telegraph Act, 1885 And section 4 thereto And sections 5 And 11 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933. Mr Mohammad Ali also relied upon the other provisions of the Act of 2001, namely, sections 4, 29, 31(C), 33, 34, sub-section 3 of sections 35, 36, 37, 55, 56 And 90 for the proposition that by the promulgation of the Act of 2001  the old laws namely, the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 have not been altogether made ineffective And a person who wants to broadcast its programme through allocation of frequency through a satellite channel must first apply to the Government for having such licence And then can apply to the BTRC for the allocation of frequency. In reply to the said submission Dr Kamal Hossain relied upon the proviso to sub-section 2 of section 3 And clause (m) of section 30 And sections 31, 35, 36 And 55 of the Act of 2001 And submitted that if those sections are read together And a cohesive meaning is given it would be found that it is not at all necessary to approach the Ministry for such licence. He further submitted that the preamble to the Act of 2001 clearly speaks about the necessity to establish an independent Commission for the purpose of development And efficient regulation of the telecommunication system And the telecommunication service in Bangladesh And matters ancillary thereto And, in fact, the Act of 2001 has created BTRC as an independent body; there cannot be any rationale in the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General that a person first has to approach the Ministry under the old laws which are too old to meet the present revolution that has taken place in the development of telecommunication And other matters ancillary thereto; the petitioner rightly approached the BTRC And it having refused to give the licence the petitioner is entitled to get a mAndate from this court as prayed for. 

 31. In order to answer the contentions raised by the learned Advocates we feel it necessary to consider the preamble of the Act of 2001 And also of the two old laws in the field namely, the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act of 1933.  38. In interpreting the provision of a statute a cohesive And workable meaning has to be given And in order to do that the provisions of the statute have to be read as a whole. It is also to be kept in mind that by giving a narrow meaning of a part of the statute the whole object And aim of the statute itself cannot be made ineffective. If the narrow meaning of the applicability of the Act in respect of the matters as mentioned in sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Act of 2001 as argued by the learned Additional Attorney-General is given the other parts of the statute namely, sections 29, 30, 31, 34, 35, 36, 55 And 56 of the Act as quoted And discussed hereinbefore shall be made ineffective. If it is held that even after the enactment of the Act of 2001 the provisions of section 4 of the Telegraph Act, 1885 And section 5 of the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 are to be resorted to by a person for the purpose of a licence in respect of the matters as mentioned in sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Act, then the very purpose of the creation of an independent commission as stated in the preamble of the Act shall be frustrated And we shall be giving back again at a time when only telegraph And other limited technology as have been used in the two old laws namely, the Telegraph Act, 1885 And the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 were invented.
